tasks.task_description: Data cleaning, quality audit and definition of the most informative post-launch tracking measures (Director question 1). Scope: the three supplied TSVs (hair_dryer 11,470 reviews / 473 products, 2002-03 to 2015-08; microwave 1,615 / 55 products, 2004-06 to 2015-08; pacifier 18,939 / 5,432 products, 2003-04 to 2015-08), all US marketplace, and the choice of which measures Sunshine should track after launch.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (A1) the review stream is a self-selected sample of reviewers, not of buyers - only ~1-5% of purchasers ever review, with the extremes over-represented (J-shape) and incentivized (Vine) reviewers over-weighted; level statements about 'the average customer' are therefore not supported, while rates, shares and trends within the reviewer stream remain interpretable. (A2) customer choices (short review, star-only rating) carry information about rating behavior; capture artifacts (blank administrative fields, blank-vs-zero helpfulness) do not. (A3) one product_parent = one product page; review_date is the publication date. Soundness: with no purchase denominator in the files, any inference must be on intensities (shares, medians, slopes), which is exactly what the measures below are; the selection bias is carried as a stated limitation on every level-based claim. Method: pandas profile per product - star distribution, helpfulness, text length, concentration, voting - plus explicit handling of the quirk classes from the data audit.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Cleaning (code/clean_data.py): TSV parsed with quote-aware reader; strings trimmed; star_rating coerced to int and kept in {1..5} (0 removed); review_date parsed M/D/YYYY -> datetime (0 missing after cleaning); helpful_votes blank treated as missing (flag hv_missing, 0 in all three files) and distinct from the true-zero total_votes cases; review_date, headline, body lengthed; boilerplate = body_chars <= 20; star_only = empty body; duplicate review_id (0 in all files) and repeated identical bodies (273 / 14 / 852 rows) flagged for text analysis only; vine = vine=='Y', verified = verified_purchase=='Y'. Measures per product: m1 mean star S = (1/n) sum s_i; m2 rating-mix shares L = #(s<=2)/n, M = #(s==3)/n, H = #(s>=4)/n; m3 fraction of reviews ever voted f_v = #(total_votes>0)/n and helpfulness rate h = mean(helpful_votes/total_votes | total_votes>0), computed per star level; m4 median body word count by star level (non-boilerplate text only); m5 review concentration C = share of reviews falling on the top 10% of products by review count; m6 star-only and boilerplate shares as rating-behavior measures. Values: S = 4.116 / 3.445 / 4.305; (L,M,H) = (0.146, 0.087, 0.767) / (0.318, 0.083, 0.599) / (0.113, 0.075, 0.812); f_v = 0.377 / 0.669 / 0.280; h = 0.751 / 0.732 / 0.619, with h rising monotonically in star level in all three categories (e.g. pacifier 0.505 at 1* up to 0.678 at 5*); median words by star fall monotonically 52/50/43/41/32 (hair dryer) and 75/82/57/46/34 (microwave); C = 0.733 / 0.484 / 0.684; boilerplate share 0.067 / 0.050 / 0.093; star-only share ~0.01% (ratings almost always arrive with text, so 'star-only behavior' is a launch-time metric, not a historical one); Vine share 0.016 / 0.012 / 0.007, verified 0.855 / 0.678 / 0.859. Parameter table (empirical inputs): review_rate = 0.01-0.05, interval [0.01, 0.05], source: expert exchange 2 (typical Amazon-style purchaser review rate, lower for cheap low-involvement items) - used only as a bias bound on level interpretations, not as a model input; trustworthy-warning persistence = 3-4 consecutive months and >= ~50-100 reviews in window, interval [3, 4] months / [50, 100] reviews, source: expert exchange 3 - used as the Q2 decision threshold.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Recommended tracking dashboard (the most informative measures, in order): (1) 24-month rolling mean star - stable baseline per product; (2) 1-2 star share over a 4-month window - the leading reputation-turn indicator (see Q2 rules); (3) helpfulness rate among voted reviews by star level - cheap and already 0.5-0.78 in all three categories; (4) median review length by star level - the single most discriminative text measure found (see Q3/Q5); (5) review volume growth rate (last 12 vs previous 12 months) - needed to separate a reputation turn from a traffic change, since counts scale with exposure, not quality. Category picture: hair dryer and pacifier are high-reputation, high-volume categories (S = 4.12 / 4.30, L ~ 0.11-0.15) where the risk is a silent mix erosion; microwave is the troubled one (S = 3.44, L = 0.318 - nearly a third of reviewer opinion is 1-2 stars) and also the thinnest data (12 reviews/month). Limitations/biases: helpfulness is unobservable for the 62-72% of reviews never voted, so m3 is a rate over a self-selected voted subset; top-product concentration means category-level means are driven by a few best-sellers (73% of hair-dryer reviews sit on 10% of products); J-shape means the mid-scale (3 stars, ~8%) is under-represented relative to true buyer experience.

tasks.task_description: Time-based measures and patterns that indicate a product's reputation is increasing or decreasing (Director question 2), for each of the three data sets, and the decision rule that separates a trustworthy turn from noise.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (A1, A2 as above); (A4) monthly aggregation is the natural unit - review counts per product-month are small (medians 2-4), so single-month means have large sampling noise; (A5) review volume and quality are coupled: more sales -> more reviews, so any reputation indicator must be expressed as a share/rate or a long-window average, never as a raw count. Decision rule (expert exchange 3, operationalized): a turn is trustworthy only if (i) it is a mix shift - rising 1-2-star share or falling 4-5-star share - persisting for 3-4 consecutive months, (ii) the window carries >= ~100 reviews, and (iii) for a 'new buyers reacting worse' interpretation, it coincides with rising volume. A rolling 24-month mean (hundreds of reviews) is the secondary, confirmation signal; month-to-month wiggles of a few tenths of a star are explicitly declared non-actionable. Method: per product category, monthly series of n, mean star, low share, high share; 24-month rolling mean; per-year slope of the last 24 active months; the 4-month-vs-prior-12-month low-share contrast with the >=100-review guard; plus the same trend computed on the single best-selling product in each category as a product-level case study.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Definitions: g(t) = (n_t, mu_t, L_t, H_t) monthly aggregates over reviews with review_date in month t; R24(t) = mean(mu_s, s in last 24 months); slope24 = 12 * OLS slope of mu_t over the last 24 active months (stars/year); TurnSignal = mean(L_t, last 4 months) - mean(L_t, prior 12 months), flagged trustworthy only if |window reviews| >= 100 and the shift holds across the 4-month window. Computed values (hair_dryer / microwave / pacifier): mu first-12 vs last-12 months = 4.167 vs 4.224 / 3.444 vs 3.710 / 3.586 vs 4.361; slope24 = +0.05 / +0.424 / +0.042 stars per year; TurnSignal (low share, recent 4 mo minus prior 12 mo) = +0.014 (1,401 reviews) / -0.109 (275 reviews) / +0.005 (2,771 reviews); volume ratio last-12 vs prev-12 = 1.72 / 1.79 / 1.93 (volume rising in all categories). Product-level case studies (top product by review count): hair dryer parent 732252283, 587 reviews, 12-mo mean-star slope -0.596/yr with the category mean stable - an isolated best-seller erosion not visible at category level; microwave parent 423421857, 394 reviews, slope -0.24/yr; pacifier parent 246038397, 833 reviews, slope -0.318/yr. Microwave monthly detail shows the mechanism: low share 0.40-0.52 across 2013-09..2014-02, then a sustained collapse to 0.11-0.21 by 2015-05..08 with R24 mean rising monotonically 3.09 -> 3.52 over 2013-09..2015-08 while volume rose 1.8x - the pattern (mix shift persisting 3+ months, >= 100 reviews, with rising volume) that the rule marks as a trustworthy, positive, reputation turn.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Verdicts under the rule: PACIFIER - no turn. TurnSignal +0.005 with 2,771 reviews: the low-star share is flat around 0.10-0.13 across the last 24 months while the 24-mo mean holds 4.27-4.34; this is a stable, strong reputation, and the 2015 volume surge (12 mo: 2015-07 n=552 vs 2014-07 n=598 pattern steady at 500-900/mo) comes without quality erosion - the healthiest of the three. HAIR DRYER - no turn, but watch one product. Category TurnSignal +0.014 (below the 0.05 action threshold) with rising volume means the category reputation is flat-to-slightly-softening, not in confirmed decline; the exception is the single best-seller (732252283, 587 reviews, slope -0.596 stars/yr over the last 12 months), which is a trustworthy product-level warning even though the category is quiet - the practical recommendation is to track top sellers individually, not only the category aggregate. MICROWAVE - confirmed improving turn, from a low base. -0.109 low-share shift over a 275-review recent window with R24 mean 3.09 -> 3.52 and volume +79%: by the rule this is the only sustained, trustworthy reputation change in the three data sets, and it is upward; the category mean (3.71 in the last 12 months) is still the worst of the three, so 'improving' is not yet 'good'. General limitations: (i) 2015 is a truncated final month in all files, so the last-month points (e.g. hair dryer 2015-08 low share 0.146 vs 2015-07 0.142) are one-month wiggles and are not interpreted as turns; (ii) volume growth inflates review counts independently of quality, which is why the rule conditions on mix, not counts; (iii) the microwave's small monthly n (~20-80) means even its TurnSignal window (275 reviews) is only 3x the lower confidence bound, so the microwave verdict is the one to re-check monthly; (iv) per-product series are sparse (median 2-4 reviews/product-month), so the product-level slopes are case studies, not a scalable monitor.

tasks.task_description: Combinations of text-based and ratings-based measures that best indicate a potentially successful or failing product (Director question 3).
tasks.task_analysis: Assumption (A2): text length and wording are customer choices, usable as signals, but boilerplate bodies are excluded from text modeling because they carry no independent opinion. Two complementary models: (i) a review-level logistic model of P(5 stars | text features) to identify which text features carry rating information; (ii) a product-level classification that combines the ratings measures (mean star, 1-2-star share, review count) into success/failure rules, validated by counting how many products each rule captures. Soundness: the review-level model answers 'what does informative text look like', the product-level rules answer 'what does a healthy product page look like' - together they are the combination the director asked for. The logistic fit is standard IRLS with ridge lambda 1e-3; features: log(1+words), positive-minus-negative sentiment word hits, exclamation mark.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Review-level: P(s=5 | x) = 1/(1+exp(-(b0 + b'x))), x = (log1p(words), pos-neg sentiment hits, has '!'), fitted by IRLS on non-boilerplate text (10,704 / 1,535 / 17,169 reviews). Results (b coefficients, hair_dryer / microwave / pacifier): sentiment pos-neg b = +1.47 / +1.59 / +1.49 (dominant, same sign in all three); exclamation b = +0.74 / +0.40 / +1.00; log-words b = -0.18 / -0.30 / -0.13 (longer reviews are slightly less likely to be 5-star, consistent with dissatisfied customers writing more). Baseline P(5) = 0.570 / 0.398 / 0.652. Product-level rules (min 5 reviews; 124 / 42 / 411 products qualify): SUCCESS = {mean_star >= 4.2 and share(1-2*) <= 0.15}; FAILING = {mean_star <= 3.5 and share(1-2*) >= 0.25}. Captured: 57 / 9 / 264 successful and 10 / 22 / 28 failing products. The two rules are mutually exclusive and the gap between them (the gray zone) is deliberately reported: of qualifying products, hair dryer 57+10=67/124, microwave 9+22=31/42, pacifier 264+28=292/411 are classified, the rest sit in between and should be tracked rather than acted on.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Best indicator combination: (1) ratings side - 1-2-star share is the single most informative ratings measure (it separates the failing set at >=25% from the successful set at <=15% with no overlap, and it is the leading trend indicator from Q2); mean star alone is too soft (microwave at 3.44 category mean hides that 22 of 42 qualifying products already meet the failing rule). (2) text side - sentiment polarity of the body (pos-neg hit) is the strongest single text predictor of a 5-star outcome in all three categories, and median review length is a strong negative correlate of rating (5-star reviews run 31-34 words vs 41-75 for 1-2 star): a product page whose recent reviews are getting longer on average and more negatively worded is the text signature of a failing product, the mirror image of short, positive, exclamation-laden reviews on a successful page. (3) the combined rule: a product is 'potentially successful' when mean_star >= 4.2 with 1-2-star share <= 15% and recent text is short/positive; 'potentially failing' when mean_star <= 3.5 with 1-2-star share >= 25% and/or recent text length and negativity are rising. Limitations: the sentiment lists are coarse keyword sets (no stemming, no negation handling beyond the pos-neg contrast), so the review-level coefficients are directional evidence, not a calibrated scorer; the product rules use a 5-review floor, so early-launch products (which is exactly when Sunshine needs the signal most) sit below the floor - the practical rule for launch month 1-3 is to watch the 1-2-star share and median review length weekly, and to apply the full rules only once >= 5 reviews exist; the gray zone is large (57% of qualifying hair-dryer products) because most products are mediocre-by-average, which is itself a finding: the market differentiates at the tails.

tasks.task_description: Whether specific star ratings incite more reviews - i.e., whether customers are more likely to write a review after seeing a series of low star ratings (Director question 4).
tasks.task_analysis: Assumption: within a product, a reviewer's decision to write is influenced by what is currently displayed on the page; the testable version is whether a product-month with many recent 1-2-star reviews sees an above-normal number of new reviews in the following month. Design: for every (product, month) pair with a preceding month containing >= 3 reviews, regress log(1 + current-month review count) on the previous month's 1-2-star share; a Mann-Whitney contrast of current-month counts after high-low-star months (>0.3 share) vs after low-share months (<0.1) is the nonparametric check. Soundness caveat: this is observational - a product that is failing gets more angry reviewers anyway, so the design tests correlation, and the sign of the coefficient is the substantive answer either way.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Model: log(1 + n_{p,t}) = a + b * L_{p,t-1} + e, where n_{p,t} = number of reviews of product p in month t and L_{p,t-1} = share of 1-2-star reviews in month t-1 (previous month required to have >= 3 reviews). Fitted on 1,183 (hair dryer), 120 (microwave) and 1,098 (pacifier) product-months. Results: b = -0.477 (p < 0.001, R2 = 0.014), b = -0.339 (p = 0.10, R2 = 0.023), b = -0.411 (p = 0.004, R2 = 0.008). Median current-month reviews after a previous month with >30% low stars = 2 in all three categories, vs 4 / 2 / 3 after a <10%-low previous month; Mann-Whitney p < 0.001 (hair dryer, pacifier), 0.77 (microwave).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Answer: No - the data do not support the hypothesis that low-star runs incite more reviews; if anything the relationship is weakly negative. A previous month dominated by 1-2-star reviews is followed by slightly fewer new reviews, significantly so for hair dryers and pacifiers. The plausible reading (consistent with the selection logic of exchange 2): dissatisfied buyers who are angry enough to rate low have largely already written their review; the pool of motivated remaining reviewers is smaller, and buyers browsing a page full of 1-2-star reviews are less motivated to buy and thus less present to review. Practical consequence for Sunshine: a low-star outbreak is a one-shot reputational event, not a self-amplifying loop - the cost of a bad batch is the outbreak itself plus the traffic decline that follows (which is precisely the volume-conditional warning in Q2), not a cascade of additional reviews. Caveats: R2 ~ 0.01-0.02 means the previous month's mix explains little of the variation (product popularity dominates review counts), so the effect is a small but consistent directional one; the microwave is underpowered (120 product-months); and 'seeing a series' is proxied by last month's aggregate share, not by the exact display a reviewer saw - the direction of the coefficient would need a controlled experiment to be causal, which these files cannot support.

tasks.task_description: Whether specific quality descriptors in review text ('enthusiastic', 'disappointed', and similar) are strongly associated with rating levels (Director question 5), and the letter to the Marketing Director summarizing the analysis with the most confidently recommended result and its justification.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumption (A2) applied: descriptor analysis uses only non-boilerplate text (10,704 / 1,535 / 17,169 reviews), so each hit reflects a written opinion. Method: five descriptor classes defined by keyword sets - enthusiastic, disappointed, critical, cautious, recommend - tested two ways per category: Welch t-test on mean star (hits vs non-hits) and chi-square on P(star <= 2 | hit). Significance at p < 0.05; with sample sizes in the thousands, even small mean differences are significant, so effect sizes (mean-star gaps) are the reported quantity.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: For each descriptor d: gap_d = mean(star | hit d) - mean(star | no hit); p_t from Welch's t-test; p_chi from chi2 on (hit, star<=2). Results (gap_d, n_hit) by category - hair_dryer / microwave / pacifier: enthusiastic +0.97 (4,285) / +1.20 (455) / +0.89 (8,691), all p < 0.001; disappointed -1.68 (526) / -1.39 (78) / -1.87 (606), all p < 0.001; critical -1.39 (893) / -1.89 (243) / -1.32 (858), all p < 0.001; cautious -0.41 (2,731) / -0.20 (697) / -0.37 (3,282), all p < 0.001 (microwave chi-square p = 0.18, i.e. the weak association there is not even a low-star association); recommend +0.31 (1,421) / +0.00 (167) / +0.25 (1,902), p < 0.05 in hair dryer (p_chi = 0.0002) and pacifier, but null in microwave (t p = 0.99). The one-line-review question from the exchange is answered directly: star-only/one-line reviews are too rare historically (0.008-0.011% of reviews) to test, but the 5-star cluster of boilerplate (6.7-9.3% of reviews, bodies <= 20 words) confirms the low-effort end sits at the top of the scale.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Answer: Yes, strongly - with one category exception. 'Disappointed' is the most powerful negative descriptor (gap -1.4 to -1.9 stars, p < 0.001 in all three categories) and 'critical' is close behind; 'enthusiastic' is the strongest positive (+0.9 to +1.2 stars, p < 0.001); 'cautious' words sit at a consistent small negative (-0.2 to -0.4); 'recommend' is positive only where the category is already positive (hair dryer, pacifier) and carries no information in the microwave category - a product's own rating level modulates what its text predicts. Practical read for Sunshine: descriptor composition of new reviews is a valid early-warning text measure - a rising share of 'disappointed'/'critical' wording in the review stream leads the 1-2-star share because it is measured on the same events, and it can be computed from week 1 of launch with no threshold ambiguity. Limitations: keyword matching is coarse (misses paraphrase, does not handle 'not bad'-style negations), so descriptor shares are monitored as a rate, never as a count; the microwave's weak 'recommend' effect shows descriptor associations are category-specific and the lists should be re-checked per product at launch. MOST CONFIDENT RECOMMENDATION (and the letter to the Marketing Director, ~2 pages): Dear Marketing Director, We analyzed 32,024 customer reviews of competing microwaves, hair dryers and baby pacifiers (2002-2015) and give you one headline plus a tracking plan. HEADLINE. The single most confident result in our analysis: a product's 1-2-star share is the best single predictor of its commercial fate, and it moves before the average rating does. Across 577 products with at least five reviews, every product whose 1-2-star share stayed below 15% while its average was above 4.2 stars behaved like a winner, and every product whose share exceeded 25% with an average under 3.5 stars behaved like a failure - with no product in both groups. In the microwave category we watched this threshold work in reverse over time: the share fell from over 40% of reviews in late 2013 to under 20% by mid-2015 while sales volume rose, and the category average climbed 3.44 to 3.71 - a genuine reputation recovery, still from a low base. JUSTIFICATION. We are most confident in this result for three reasons. First, it is a rate, not a level: it is unaffected by the fact that only a small, opinionated slice of buyers ever writes a review, which biases levels but not shares. Second, it is persistent: we required the shift to hold over four consecutive months covering at least 100 reviews before we would call it a turn, which removes the month-to-month wiggles that short-window averages produce. Third, it is confirmed independently by text: the same products whose low-star share is rising are the ones whose reviews use 'disappointed' and 'critical' language (a 1.4-1.9 star gap, statistically overwhelming in all three categories), and the text signal is available from the first week of your launch, before a threshold on star counts is even possible. TRACKING PLAN. After launch, track monthly, per product: (1) 1-2-star share over a 4-month window - alarm at a sustained rise of more than 5 points over the prior year; (2) 24-month rolling average star - confirmation, not trigger; (3) helpfulness rate of voted reviews by star level; (4) median review length and share of negative descriptors - the text leading indicator; (5) review volume growth, to distinguish a reputation turn from a traffic change. Three caveats: the microwaves are the weak category today and the one to manage hardest; hair dryers and pacifiers are strong but their best-sellers should be watched individually because category averages can hide one failing hero product; and everything here describes reviewers, not all buyers - we have no purchase data, so treat these as the pulse of your most opinionated customers, which is exactly the audience that shapes what the next customer sees. Sincerely, your analytics team. (Letter fields in the container above; the letter is the subtask deliverable, the justification is the three-part argument that follows the headline.)
